newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU swing to left will prompt refocus on jobs.
newsitem.headline: EU swing to left will prompt refocus on jobs.

text.p: Europe's shift to the political centre-left, while unsettling prospects for monetary union, could spur the European Union towards deeper integration on social issues, such as jobs, political analysts said on Monday.
Sweeping election victories for France's Socialist Party and Britain's Labour Party in the past month mean that 13 of the 15 EU member governments now include the centre or left.
Only Germany and Spain have conservative administrations.

Analysts said the ascendency of the left in Europe would make employment a key focus in future EU negotiations, rather than a dogmatic adherence to monetary union criteria which has forced governments to adopt unpopular austerity programmes.

France's Socialists claim their stunning win in Sunday's parliamentary election was a mandate for a new direction in European policy. Last month, Tony Blair promised a "fresh start" for Britain in Europe after 18 years of Conservative nay-saying on closer integration.

"Clearly the swing to the left could be said to reflect the fact that unemployment is everybody's primary problem," said Peter Ludlow, director at the Centre for European Policy Studies, an independent Brussels-based think-tank.

He noted that the most successful EU states in terms of job creation and growth were the model Maastricht economies, such as the Dutch, Danes, Irish and Luxembourg, "those that have played Maastricht by the book."

These smaller EU members have switched to a mix of fiscal propriety and consensus politics -- adopting strict monetary and fiscal policies coupled with social consensus aimed at creating a new, more flexible labour market.

"Europe has certain things Europe can do and both theory and experience suggest that those who take advantage of the European dimension and adopt enlightened policies at local level will in fact do very well," Ludlow said.
"What Europe cannot be is an alibi for incompetent national governments who won't do anything else."

Analysts do not expect the French result to have a major impact on an Amsterdam summit in two weeks which is expected to agree landmark reforms to take the bloc into the next century prepared for an ambitious eastward expansion.
"I don't think for a moment that the French government will try to reopen much. Everybody wants this (inter-governmental conference (IGC)) over," said one EU diplomat.
A new Amsterdam treaty is likely to include some words on unemployment as part of the Social Chapter, supporting basic workplace rules and conditions.
"An employment chapter will be held up as 'we're doing something for Europe', but the main danger is that it might give the impression that Europe can do things that it can't do," said Ludlow.
German left-wing opposition leader Oskar Lafontaine said he expected Lionel Jospin's win in France to refocus Europe's drive against joblessness, which currently tops 18 million.
"With it are linked the people's hopes for a reduction in unemployment and for more social justice," he said.
EU diplomats welcomed the French Socialists' clear victory which would help bolster stability at a time when Europe was trying to forge closer ties and reform for the future.
But, while jobs will be given a higher priority, the French result has thrown prospects of a credible monetary union into serious doubt.
Jospin is committed to the euro, but not to the strict criteria attached to it, prompting many to believe the euro launch will be fudged to allow wider single currency membership.
But this could be torpedoed by German demands to delay the project rather than see the planned euro kick off as a weaker currency than the German mark.
Economists, however, reckon the French Socialists are unlikely to take big risks with EMU plans, wanting to establish their credibility in the eyes of financial markets.
